inventory.value: Enteral Nutrition
Clinical nutrition support
Translate gastrointestinal function, access, formula composition, medication handling, and monitoring into a safe enteral nutrition plan.
Indications and timing
Access and delivery
Formula selection
Medication safety
Monitoring and complications
Determine when enteral nutrition is appropriate and when feeding should be delayed or withheld.
Select an access site and administration method that match duration, gastric function, aspiration risk, and patient goals.
Compare formula composition and calculate delivery, free water, and supplemental flush requirements.
Administer medications through enteral access without compromising the drug, formula, or tube.
Recognize signs that warrant assessment for intolerance, refeeding risk, aspiration, contamination, or mechanical complications.
The Enteral Decision
Use the gastrointestinal tract when it can safely receive and absorb nutrients, but separate a functioning gut from a patient who is not yet adequately resuscitated.
Indications and goals
Hemodynamic stability
Contraindications
Early critical care feeding
Before writing a feeding order, state why oral intake is inadequate, whether the gut is usable, whether perfusion is adequate, and what clinical outcome the therapy should support.
A functional, safe gut supports enteral nutrition; compare routes within the applicable clinical setting.
Nutrition risk and expected inadequacy guide initiation.
Withhold feeding for suspected bowel ischemia, complete intestinal obstruction, or hemodynamic instability; reassess before initiation or resumption.
Early feeding is a monitored strategy, not an automatic full-rate order.
Access and Route Selection
Access is chosen by expected duration, anatomy, gastric emptying, aspiration risk, procedural burden, and the therapies that must pass through the tube.
Gastric versus postpyloric
Nasal versus percutaneous
Placement confirmation
ENFit safety
Choose the least invasive route that can reliably deliver the prescribed therapy, then build a placement, securement, skin care, and reassessment plan around it.
Gastric access permits bolus, intermittent, or continuous feeding when function, tolerance, and aspiration risk allow.
Postpyloric access is selected for a clinical reason, not by habit.
Confirm initial placement before use and reassess possible migration.
Use enteral-specific connectors to reduce the risk of wrong-route connections.
Delivery and the Feeding Prescription
The prescription links a daily nutrient and fluid target to a formula, route, rate, schedule, flush plan, and advancement strategy.
Bolus, intermittent, and continuous delivery
Daily volume targets
Rate calculations
Advancement and interruptions
Every order should make the intended daily volume visible. Calculate what will actually be delivered after holds, procedures, medication windows, and pump downtime.
Bolus feeding is generally a gastric strategy.
Rate multiplied by hours equals delivered volume.
Advancement follows tolerance and refeeding risk.
Track prescribed volume against actual delivery.
Formula Selection and Hydration
Match formula composition to nutrient, volume, digestion, absorption, electrolyte, and tolerance needs; greater complexity does not establish greater benefit.
Polymeric and peptide-based formulas
Caloric density
Fiber and disease-specific products
Free water and renal solute load

inventory.value: Start with physiology and the nutrition prescription. Product marketing cannot substitute for an assessment of protein, calories, fluid, electrolytes, fiber, absorption, cost, and evidence.
Polymeric formula is a reasonable starting point when digestion and absorption are intact.
Calculate formula water from product composition and the volume actually delivered.
Specialty formulas require a patient-specific rationale.
Formula volume and water volume are not interchangeable.
Medication Administration Through Enteral Access
Safe medication delivery requires a dosage-form review, absorption-site review, drug-specific feeding plan, and flush sequence for every administration.
Do-not-crush formulations
Drug and nutrient interactions
Flush sequence
Tube site and dosage form
Do not ask only whether a tablet can fit through a tube. Ask whether the dosage form can be altered, whether the drug can be absorbed beyond the tube tip, and whether feeding changes exposure.
Check product-specific instructions before altering or administering any dosage form through a tube.
Give medications separately from formula and from one another.
Use drug-specific feeding holds rather than a universal rule.
The tube tip can change drug absorption and effect.
Monitoring and Complication Prevention
Tolerance is a clinical pattern. Integrate delivered volume, symptoms, examination, stool, fluid balance, glucose, electrolytes, access integrity, and infection risk.
Aspiration prevention
Diarrhea and intolerance
Tube obstruction and displacement
Refeeding and metabolic monitoring
When a problem appears, assess gastrointestinal, metabolic, mechanical, medication-related, and infectious causes. Respond promptly to urgent findings and reassess the feeding plan.
Aspiration prevention uses several coordinated measures.
A residual value must be interpreted in clinical context.
Assess medications as possible causes of diarrhea and tube obstruction.
Monitor what was delivered, not only what was ordered.
